source.title: Mixture-of-Experts with Expert Choice Routing
source.authors: Yan-Qi Zhou; Tao Lei; Han-Chu Liu; Nan Du; Yan-Ping Huang; Vincent Y. Zhao; Andrew M. Dai; Zhi-Feng Chen; Quoc V. Le; J. Laudon

record.file_problem: No substantial problem; the extracted text contains minor formatting and table-layout artifacts.
record.tranche_reason: The study reports expert-count scaling and downstream results for sparsely activated MoE language models, a new setting for the scaling findings. It does not fit or test the original power-law equations.
record.gate_note: The paper cites prior power-law scaling findings in its introduction, but those cited findings are not this study's results. Its own expert-count sweep reports evaluation perplexity improving with more experts; the figures do not provide extractable numerical values or a power-law fit. Downstream averages are reported for several model sizes.
record.test_reason: The paper is mainly about an MoE routing method, but it reports its own results at several scales. These are an expert-count sweep of eval perplexity (16→128 experts at fixed 145M activated parameters, figure only) and downstream averages across those sizes and an 8B/64E model. The authors state explicitly that better perplexity with more experts does not translate into better downstream results. That bears on V6 in a new setting (sparse MoE). There is no power-law fit, so V1 is touched only qualitatively.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that expert-choice routing gives over 2× faster training convergence than GShard top-2 and Switch top-1. They report stronger GLUE/SuperGLUE fine-tuning at equal compute, and 8B/64E beats dense 8B on 7 of 11 tasks. They note perplexity scales strongly with expert count, but the 100M/32E setting is best downstream, so better perplexity does not always yield better downstream performance.
record.recipe_differences: Studies a new MoE routing method and compares its training and downstream results; it does not reproduce the scaling-law fitting recipe.
record.method_sensitivity: Expert count changes evaluation perplexity and downstream average accuracy; limiting experts per token and capacity factor also changes reported outcomes, but those ablations do not test fitted scaling laws.
record.problems: The expert-count evaluation-perplexity results are shown in figures without extractable values, and the paper does not fit power laws. Downstream results use selected tasks and model settings; the paper says it reports averaged results for other experiments only in a limited fashion.
record.rows_left_out: No additional rows left out. Other routing, capacity-factor, and per-token expert-cap ablations concern routing choices rather than the claim versions' power-law or compute-optimal allocation statements.

untested.parts: No power-law fit or exponent. Tokens and compute are not varied. Dense parameter scaling is not swept. The range is under one order of magnitude of total parameters, at fixed activated compute.
No other modalities or regimes tested for power-law form.
No fitted predictive relation between loss or scale and downstream accuracy. Only 11 GLUE/SuperGLUE tasks are used, with mostly single fine-tuning runs.
No comparison of fitting or setup choices on exponents.

missing.what: GShard top-2 downstream averages across expert count: 32E 83.5, 64E 82.2, 128E 81.3. The same reversal as EC.
Switch Transformer top-1 downstream averages: 32E 80.6, 64E 78.4, 128E 81.0 (non-monotonic). 8B/64E: ST 88.9, GS 90.3.
Dense vs MoE pretraining perplexity at 100M and 8B, showing perplexity improves with expert capacity and model size (figure only).

record.verdict_notes: The paper's primary aim is routing efficiency, not scaling laws. The V1-relevant sweep is figure-only and short-range, so no V1 verdict is given. The V6 evidence rests on single fine-tuning runs; only the 100M/64E appendix variants report three-run averages. The text alternates between 'training' and 'eval' perplexity for Fig. 2(b); the axis reads Eval Perplexity.

versions.untested_parts: Tests evaluation perplexity while increasing MoE expert count at fixed expert size and activated parameters. Does not fit a power law or report exponents; does not vary training tokens or compute independently, test dense-model parameter scaling, or establish the claimed range of several orders of magnitude.
No small-run fit is used to predict the loss of much larger runs.
No fixed-compute search for a loss-minimising parameter/token allocation or power-law allocation trend.
No controlled comparison of depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
No power-law tests in other modalities or the listed repeated-data, fine-tuning, or transfer regimes.

Reports downstream benchmark averages at selected model sizes and notes that better pretraining perplexity does not always translate to better downstream performance. Does not fit a predictive relationship between pretraining loss and downstream performance or test a broad range of downstream tasks.
Does not compare fitted scaling exponents or compute-optimal splits under alternative parameter-counting, fitting, data, or schedule choices, or test departures from a single power law.

relationships.condition: MoE with 100M expert size, expert count 32→64→128 at fixed activated compute (EC-CF2 and GShard top-2)
relationships.reason: Pretraining perplexity improves with experts (R1–R8), yet EC-CF2 downstream average falls 85.0→84.0→82.6 (R9–R11). GS top-2 falls 83.5→82.2→81.3 (Table 2, not in rows). Authors say perplexity gains do not always translate downstream. These are single runs.
relationships.display_finding: Increasing experts from 32 to 64 to 128 improved perplexity but reduced downstream averages from 85.0 to 84.0 to 82.6 for EC-CF2 and from 83.5 to 82.2 to 81.3 for GShard top-2 in single runs.

tranche.reason: Section 4.4 explicitly tests whether improved pretraining perplexity translates downstream and reports the opposite ordering across expert counts. This directly qualifies V6, meeting the T5 definition.
